concept.body: Perimeter on the plane: walk the vertices IN ORDER, computing each side with the distance formula (axis-aligned sides read directly as coordinate differences), and sum — including the final side back to the start. Keep radicals exact until the last step: √20 + √20 = 2√20 = 4√5, never premature decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: 7 = 3 + 4 forgets the trip home — the hypotenuse is 5: total 12.
5 is only the hypotenuse — the lap is 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.

steps.body: Perimeter is the distance formula on a lap: sum every side, walking the vertices IN ORDER. Two disciplines carry the chapter — keep radicals EXACT until the final step (√20 + √20 = 2√20, never 4.47 + 4.47), and never skip a side: n vertices, n sides, back to the start.

explanationVariants: Sides: (0,0)→(6,0) is 6; (6,0)→(6,8) is 8; the hypotenuse home is √(36 + 64) = 10.

commonErrors.feedback: 14 = 6 + 8 stops before the trip home — the hypotenuse √(6² + 8²) = 10 completes the lap: 24.
48 doubles — or computes 6 × 8 area-style. The lap is 6 + 8 + 10 = 24.
10 is just the hypotenuse — add the two axis-aligned legs: 24.

explanationVariants: All four sides of the rhombus square to 25 — chapter 3's own figure.

widget.prompt: The rhombus (0, 0), (5, 0), (8, 4), (3, 4) from last chapter. Perimeter = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 25 is one SQUARED side — root first (5), then lap: 4 × 5 = 20.
10 counts two sides — a rhombus laps all four: 20.
100 sums the four squared sides — root before summing: 4√25 = 20.

steps.body: Mixed laps demand exact bookkeeping. The trapezoid (0,0), (8,0), (6,4), (2,4): bases 8 and 4 are free reads; each leg is √(2² + 4²) = √20 = 2√5. Perimeter: 12 + 4√5 exactly — decimalize (≈ 20.94) only at the very end, if at all.

commonErrors.feedback: 16.47 counts one leg — the trapezoid has TWO congruent legs of √20: 12 + 2√20 ≈ 20.94.
24 is this trapezoid's AREA ((8+4)/2 × 4) — the perimeter walks the boundary: ≈ 20.94.
20 = 8 + 4 + 4 + 4 reads the legs as height 4 — they slant: √(2² + 4²) each. ≈ 20.94.

widget.prompt: A square's four sides each measure √18. Best form for the perimeter?

choices.label: 4√18 = 12√2 — simplified exact radical, decimalized only if the task demands it
choices.feedback: √18 = 3√2, so 4(3√2) = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 — exact form survives further algebra; early decimals compound rounding.
Rounding √18 to 4.24 first LOSES precision (true value ≈ 16.9706) — keep 12√2 until the end.

choices.label: √72, by adding under the root
choices.feedback: √18 + √18 ≠ √36 — radicals don't add under the root. 4√18 = 12√2.

widget.successFeedback: √18 = 3√2, so 4(3√2) = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 — exact form survives further algebra; early decimals compound rounding.
widget.explorationFeedback: Open at least two coordinate-proof states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Inspect the coordinate invariants, then choose the supported conclusion.

widget.prompt: Triangle (−3, 0), (3, 0), (0, 4) — the symmetric placement from last chapter. Perimeter = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 sums the two slants (5 + 5) — the 6-unit base completes the lap: 16.
11 = 6 + 5 walks one slant — symmetry gives TWO: 6 + 5 + 5 = 16.

hints: Walk the five vertices in order — five sides, including the return to the start.

widget.prompt: A pentagon-shaped yard has corners (0,0), (9,0), (9,5), (5,8), (0,8). Fence the whole boundary: total length = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 27 misses the (9,5)→(5,8) diagonal — it's a 3-4-5 in disguise: √(16+9) = 5. Total 32.
24 = 9 + 5 + 5 + 5 stops before the last side home — the (0,8)→(0,0) side adds 8: total 32.
33.4 misprices the diagonal as √(4² + 5²) ≈ 6.4 — the drop is 8 − 5 = 3: √25 = 5, total 32.

takeaways: Perimeter = ordered sum of side distances — n vertices, n sides, home again.
Keep radicals exact (√20 = 2√5); decimalize once, at the end.
Axis-aligned sides are free reads; diagonals go through the distance formula.
